name: Tailscale
summary: A node agent and encrypted mesh VPN that separates control-plane coordination from the WireGuard peer data plane, with direct and DERP-assisted peer paths selected by the local transport engine.

features.name: Local agent as composition boundary
features.description: The LocalBackend is the node-agent boundary that coordinates the control client, network-map updates, WireGuard engine, route/DNS integration, and local clients. It is an orchestration boundary rather than the wire protocol itself.
benefits: Presents one lifecycle boundary for local node state and network configuration
Keeps local control, data-plane, and management concerns connected through explicit interfaces
costs: The agent coordinates many asynchronous subsystems and must reconcile control updates with live packet state
A local API or client operation can observe transitions while network reconfiguration is in progress

features.name: WireGuard peer data plane
features.description: The wgengine interface owns peer session state and packet-path configuration. Reconfiguring it from a control-provided network map updates WireGuard peers and kernel or userspace routes; application control messages are outside this packet data path.
benefits: Uses WireGuard cryptographic sessions for peer-to-peer encrypted traffic
Separates packet forwarding and peer route state from coordination messages
costs: Peer reachability depends on endpoint discovery and path conditions outside the engine interface
Network-map changes require synchronization between control state, routes, and live peers

features.name: Control client and relay-capable path selection
features.description: The control client obtains coordination state over the Tailscale control protocol, while magicsock selects direct peer paths when possible and can use DERP relay connections when direct paths fail. DERP relays carry encrypted peer traffic; they are transport relays rather than the control authority.
benefits: Allows coordination and encrypted peer transport to survive restrictive or changing networks
Makes direct, NAT-traversed, and relay-assisted paths interchangeable at the peer transport boundary
costs: Control reachability and peer reachability have separate failure modes
Relay use adds latency and relay dependency when direct paths are unavailable

mathematical_views.question: Which local components coordinate membership and route state, and which components carry encrypted peer packets?
assumptions: LocalBackend is a coordinator vertex; control client, network-map state, WireGuard engine, and path manager are distinct vertices
An edge from control state to engine configuration represents an update, not packet forwarding
The view abstracts server-side control implementation and WireGuard primitive internals

mathematical_views.question: How does a peer transport move among direct, NAT-traversed, and DERP-assisted paths while preserving the encrypted peer boundary?
assumptions: Path candidates and peer sessions are implementation state; each selected path carries encrypted peer traffic
The model does not claim a particular path is always available or optimal
DERP is modeled as a relay transport and not as a trust authority for plaintext traffic

mathematical_views.question: How do control-plane network-map observations become WireGuard peer and route configuration?
assumptions: A network-map update is an input to local reconciliation
Reconciliation may update routes and peers incrementally or wholly depending on engine implementation
The relation does not prove convergence time or availability
